meta.title: English Verb Patterns Test (B1-B2) - Food and Cooking
meta.description: A comprehensive test covering English verb patterns and gerunds themed around Food and Cooking, combining at least two or more topics per question.
meta.info: This test includes 30 correction-type questions focusing on combined B1-B2 level grammar structures involving verb patterns, gerunds, infinitives, and related topics.
meta.author: Qwen3.7

explanation.text: The verb 'enjoy' is followed by a gerund ('baking'), and 'avoid' is also followed by a gerund ('use' becomes 'using', so 'avoids using').
explanation.concept: Verbs followed by gerunds
examples: I enjoy cooking, but I avoid eating raw meat.

explanation.text: 'Stop to do' means to pause an action to do something else, while 'forget to do' means failing to perform an action.
explanation.concept: Change in meaning with stop and forget
examples: He stopped to check the oven, but forgot to turn it off.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form (may contain 0, 1 or multiple errors). If no error, choose No Error.

explanation.text: 'Encourage' takes an object + to-infinitive ('staff to wash'). After the preposition 'before', we use a gerund ('handling'), so 'to' is removed.
explanation.concept: Object + to-infinitive and preposition + gerund
examples: She encouraged him to try before giving up.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form (may contain 0, 1 or multiple errors). If no error, choose No Error.

explanation.text: The perfect participle 'Having tasted' is used for an action completed before the main verb. 'Must have been' is a modal perfect passive for deduction.
explanation.concept: Perfect participle and modal perfect passive
explanation.formula: Having + past participle, subject + modal + have + been + past participle
examples: Having eaten the cake, she knew it must have been baked fresh.

explanation.text: 'Mind' is followed by a gerund ('chopping'), so 'to' is removed. 'Refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to clean').
explanation.concept: Specific verb patterns
examples: I don't mind waiting, but I refuse to pay extra.

explanation.text: 'Remember + gerund' refers to a past memory. 'Forget + to-infinitive' refers to failing to perform an action.
explanation.concept: Change in meaning with remember and forget
explanation.formula: Remember + verb-ing (past memory); Forget + to-infinitive (failed action)
examples: I remember locking the door, but I forgot to turn off the lights.

explanation.text: 'Need' can be followed by a gerund to express a passive meaning ('needs baking'). 'Risk' is always followed by a gerund ('burning').
explanation.concept: Need + gerund (passive meaning) and risk + gerund
explanation.formula: Subject + need + verb-ing; Subject + risk + verb-ing
examples: The car needs washing, and it risks rusting if left outside.

explanation.text: 'Appreciate' is followed by a gerund ('having'). 'Promise' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to accommodate').
explanation.concept: Specific verb patterns
examples: We appreciate hearing from you and promise to reply soon.

explanation.text: 'Make' and 'let' are causative verbs followed by an object and the base form of the verb (without 'to').
explanation.concept: Make/let + object + base verb
explanation.formula: Make/Let + object + base verb; Preposition + verb-ing
examples: She made him clean the room before letting him play.

explanation.text: 'Try + to-infinitive' means to attempt something difficult. 'Can't help' is an expression followed by a gerund ('crying').
explanation.concept: Try (attempt) and can't help (unable to stop)
examples: I tried to lift the box, but I couldn't help dropping it.

explanation.text: A gerund ('Learning') is preferred as the subject of a sentence describing a general activity. 'Require' is followed by a gerund ('practicing').
explanation.concept: Gerund as subject and require + gerund
examples: Reading requires focusing your attention.

explanation.text: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund ('tasting') or a that-clause, not a to-infinitive. 'Might have been' is a modal perfect passive.
explanation.concept: Suggest + gerund and modal perfect passive
explanation.formula: Suggest + verb-ing; Modal + have + been + past participle
examples: I suggest checking the oil, as it might have been changed recently.

explanation.text: 'Decide' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to book'). 'Avoid' is followed by a gerund ('waiting').
explanation.concept: Decide + to-infinitive and avoid + gerund
examples: We decided to leave early to avoid getting stuck in traffic.

explanation.text: 'Allow' takes an object + to-infinitive ('interns to observe'). 'Prohibit' takes an object + from + gerund ('from touching').
explanation.concept: Allow + object + to-infinitive and prohibit + object + from + gerund
explanation.formula: Allow + object + to-infinitive; Prohibit + object + from + verb-ing
examples: They allowed us to enter but prohibited us from taking photos.

explanation.text: 'Afford' and 'plan' are both followed by a to-infinitive ('to buy', 'to grow').
explanation.concept: Verbs followed by to-infinitives
examples: I can't afford to buy it, so I plan to save money.

explanation.text: 'Claim' is followed by a perfect infinitive ('to have followed') to refer to a past action. 'Deny' is followed by a gerund ('using').
explanation.concept: Claim + perfect infinitive and deny + gerund
explanation.formula: Claim + to have + past participle; Deny + verb-ing
examples: He claimed to have seen it, but denied taking it.

explanation.text: 'Look forward to' is a phrasal verb where 'to' is a preposition, so it takes a gerund ('hosting'). 'Hope' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to impress').
explanation.concept: Look forward to + gerund and hope + to-infinitive
explanation.formula: Look forward to + verb-ing; Hope + to-infinitive
examples: I look forward to seeing you and hope to meet your family.

explanation.text: 'Intend' is typically followed by a to-infinitive ('to reduce'). 'Mean' (in the sense of 'involve') is followed by a gerund ('cutting').
explanation.concept: Intend + to-infinitive and mean + gerund
examples: I intend to study, which means giving up parties.

explanation.text: 'Dislike' is followed by a gerund. In the passive voice, this becomes 'being interrupted'. 'Try' is followed by a to-infinitive.
explanation.concept: Dislike + passive gerund and try + to-infinitive
explanation.formula: Dislike + being + past participle; Try + to-infinitive
examples: She dislikes being watched while she is trying to work.

explanation.text: 'Admit' is followed by a gerund ('making'). 'Manage' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to save').
explanation.concept: Admit + gerund and manage + to-infinitive
examples: He admitted breaking the vase but managed to fix it.

explanation.text: 'Insist' is followed by the preposition 'on' + gerund ('on paying'). 'Refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to let').
explanation.concept: Insist on + gerund and refuse + to-infinitive
examples: She insisted on helping, refusing to leave early.

explanation.text: 'Keep' is followed by a gerund ('experimenting'). 'Fail' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to achieve').
explanation.concept: Keep + gerund and fail + to-infinitive
examples: He kept trying, but failed to win the race.

explanation.text: 'Advise' takes an object + to-infinitive ('him to eat'). 'Recommend' is followed by a gerund ('avoiding').
explanation.concept: Advise + object + to-infinitive and recommend + gerund
examples: The doctor advised him to rest, recommending taking vitamins.

explanation.text: 'Regret + to-infinitive' is used for formal announcements of bad news. 'Consider' is followed by a gerund ('closing').
explanation.concept: Regret (formal) + to-infinitive and consider + gerund
examples: We regret to inform you that we are considering cancelling the event.

explanation.concept: Gerund as subject and require + gerund

explanation.concept: Suggest + gerund and offer + to-infinitive

explanation.concept: Hope + to-infinitive and miss + gerund

explanation.text: 'Avoid' is followed by a gerund ('consuming'). Modal verbs like 'must' are followed by the base form of the verb ('check') without 'to'.
explanation.concept: Avoid + gerund and modal + base verb
examples: I avoid driving at night, so I must take the bus.

explanation.concept: Expect + to-infinitive and anticipate + gerund
examples: We expect to finish soon, anticipating having time to rest.

explanation.text: The perfect participle 'Having won' is used for an action completed before the main verb. 'Decide' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to open').
